text: On December sixth the division broke out of Hagaru-ri. It took nearly two days of hard fighting to cover the eleven miles to Koto-ri. Ten thousand men in a column that stretched for miles. At Koto-ri the legendary Colonel Lewis Chesty Puller held the town with the First Marines. He is credited with a famous line about being surrounded. They are on our left. They are on our right. They are in front of us. They are behind us. They can't get away this time. But at Koto-ri the Marines faced a problem that no amount of courage could solve. South of the town the road dropped into Funchilin Pass. A steep descent toward the coastal plain. At one point the road crossed a narrow gap above the pipes of a hydroelectric power plant. The Chinese had blown the bridge there. The gap was about twenty-nine feet wide. On one side rose a cliff. On the other side was a sheer drop. Without that bridge no truck and no tank and no gun could pass. Fourteen thousand men and well over a thousand vehicles would be trapped on the plateau. The division engineer Lieutenant Colonel John Partridge had an answer. No one had ever tried it in combat before. They would drop a bridge from the sky. In Japan Air Force crews loaded steel bridge sections onto C-one-nineteen Flying Boxcar transports. Each section weighed about two and a half tons. A test drop smashed one section into the ground. So they switched to larger parachutes. On December seventh eight sections floated down over Koto-ri. One was damaged on landing. One drifted into Chinese lines. The rest landed where they were needed. It was enough. But first the Marines had to take the heights above the pass. On the night of December eighth a battalion of the First Marines climbed toward a peak called Hill ten-eighty-one in a blinding blizzard. They attacked Chinese positions in the snow. The fighting lasted into the next day. When it ended the high ground belonged to the Marines. On December ninth the engineers hauled the bridge sections down the road on trucks. They laid the steel across the gap. The span was barely wide enough. Tanks could ride on the two steel treadways. Jeeps needed wooden panels laid between them. One wrong move and a vehicle would tumble into the gorge below. That night the column began to cross. Trucks. Artillery. Ambulances. Tanks at the rear. Thousands of Korean refugees followed behind the Marines in the snow. The impossible had happened. A bridge had fallen from the sky and an entire division had walked across it. Below the pass the road opened toward the sea. Army troops waited at the bottom. By December eleventh the last Marines had come down from the mountains.
